# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## Project Summary:

This study looks at owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at different sites in and around Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area. The goal is to see how limpet size, population density, and territory size vary between locations and years. We also want to find out if larger limpets tend to have larger territories and whether limpet populations differ between sites with different levels of human impact.

Data were collected from 2022 to 2025 at Corona del Mar, Treasure Cove, Heisler Park, and Shaws Cove. We measured limpet shell lengths, counted limpets along transects, and collected data on limpet territories. Using R, we made graphs and calculated averages, standard deviations, and standard errors to compare the data. We also used t-tests, ANOVA, and linear regression to look for differences between sites and years and to examine the relationship between limpet body mass and territory size.

By comparing these sites and years, we hope to better understand how owl limpet populations vary and whether limpet size and territory size are related. The results may also help us understand how human activity could affect these populations.You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

- 2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

- 2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

- 2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

- 2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

```{r}
load(file = "Data/SizeData_2022_2025.Rdata")

SizeData_2022_2025
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(site, year, transect_num, transect_length_m) |>
  count(site) |>
  mutate(density = (n/(transect_length_m*2)))
  
# Group the data by site, year, transect number, and transect length

Limpet_Density
```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

The transects were similar in size which meant the densities at Treasure Cove did not have a distribution spread. They were all 5 meters at Treasure Cove.

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}
# Calculate limpet density for each site, year, and transect
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |>
  
  # Group observations by site, year, transect number, and transect length
  group_by(site, year, transect_num, transect_length_m) |>
  
  # Count the number of limpets in each group
  count(site) |>
  
  # Calculate limpet density per square meter
  # Assumes transects are 2 meters wide
  mutate(density = n / (transect_length_m * 2))

# Calculate the mean limpet density across all observations
mean(Limpet_Density$density, na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate the standard deviation of limpet density
sd(Limpet_Density$density, na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate the standard error of the mean (SEM)
# 1746 is the assumed sample size
sd(Limpet_Density$density, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(1746)

```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# Calculate mean limpet density, standard deviation, sample size,
# and standard error for each site and year
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |>
  
  # Group the data by site and year
  group_by(site, year) |>
  
  # Calculate summary statistics for each group
  summarize(
    mean_density = round(mean(density, na.rm = TRUE), 1), # Mean density, rounded to 1 decimal place
    
    sd_density = sd(density, na.rm = TRUE), # Standard deviation of density
    
    n = n(), # Number of rows in each site-year group
    
    se_density = round(sd_density / sqrt(n), 1) # Standard error, rounded to 1 decimal place
  )

# Display the summary table in a nicely formatted format
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)
```

#### 2.4 Make three graphs to visualize the difference in density between the two sites.

Boxplot, using the `Limpet_density` object, using fill for year. Label the Y-axis to say "Limpets per square meter".

```{r}
# Calculate limpet density for each transect
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |>
  
  # Group observations by site, year, transect number, and transect length
  group_by(site, year, transect_num, transect_length_m) |>
  
  # Count the number of limpets recorded in each transect
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
```

A column plot with errorbars, and fill = year, using your new `LimpetPopSummary` object. Make sure to label the y-axis appropriately.

```{r}
# Create a bar plot of mean limpet density by site and year
LimpetPopSummary |>
  ggplot() +
  
  # Set site on the x-axis, mean density on the y-axis,
  # and use different fill colors for each year
  aes(x = site, y = mean_density, fill = year) +
  
  # Create bars showing mean limpet density
  # Dodge the bars so different years appear side by side
  geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
  
  # Add error bars showing the mean ± standard error
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = mean_density - se_density, # Lower limit: mean minus SE
```


Which plot do you find the most informative and useful and why?

I find the boxplot the most informative because it compares limpet density between sites and years. It shows the median, spread, and potential outliers, making it easier to see differences in density.

Based on these plots, does your data meet assumptions for a t-test?

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)?

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population?

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)?

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

The data meets the continuous data assumption because limpet density (limpets per square meter) is a continuous measurement. However, it is uncertain whether the transects were randomly sampled, and the boxplots would need to be checked to determine whether the groups have similar variances. The normality of the residuals is also uncertain, especially if the data are skewed or contain outliers. Overall, the data may meet some assumptions for a t-test, but the variance and normality assumptions should be checked before proceeding.

```{r t-test}
ShawsHeislerDensity
```

Explain the results of this t-test. Are you surprised by this result, given the figure you made above? Why do you think the results are what they are?

The t-test showed that there was no statistically significant difference in average limpet density between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove (t=−1.1649t = -1.1649, df=14.466df = 14.466, p=0.2629p = 0.2629). I am not very surprised by this result if the figure showed similar densities or overlapping distributions at the two sites. The results may be due to natural variation in limpet density between transects and variation within each site, making the difference between the averages too small to be statistically significant.

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
# Test for homogeneity of variance using an F-test

# Filter the dataset to include only Corona del Mar and Treasure Cove
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |>
  filter(site == "Corona del Mar" | site == "Treasure Cove")

# Display the filtered dataset
CDM_TC_Sizes


# Fit a linear model to examine shell length differences between sites
# Shell length is the response variable, and site is the explanatory variable
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)


# Plot residuals against fitted values to check model assumptions
# Look for patterns, curves, or changes in the spread of residuals
plot(model, which = 1)


# Perform an F-test to compare shell-length variances between the two sites
# Null hypothesis (H0): The population variances are equal
# Alternative hypothesis (H1): The population variances are different
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# Interpretation:
# If p-value < 0.05, reject H0 and conclude that the variances differ.
# If p-value >= 0.05, there is insufficient evidence that the variances differ.

# NOTE: If variances are unequal, Welch's t-test is appropriate
# for comparing the means of two independent groups.
# Welch's t-test is the default in R when using t.test().
```

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

  It is not normal, the variances differ by low p-value.

```{r}
# Test the normality assumption

# Create a Q-Q plot to visually assess whether the model residuals
# approximately follow a normal distribution
plot(model, which = 2)

# Conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test to statistically test
# whether the model residuals are consistent with normality
shapiro.test(model$residuals)
```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes, Var.equal = TRUE)
```

## Part 4: Territory Size

#### 4.1 Territory Data

Clean up and combine the 2023, 2024 and 2025 data for Territories:

```{r}
# Load the dataset containing territory data from all sites
load(file = "Data/All_Territories.Rdata")

# Load the Fenberg territory dataset
load(file = "Data/FenbergTerr.Rdata")


# Display the first six rows of the All_Territories dataset
# to inspect its structure and contents
head(All_Territories)


# Create a cleaned dataset containing only the selected columns
Cleaned_Territories_Final <- All_Territories |>
  
  # Keep the year, site, location, number of squares,
  # and territory size in millimeters
  select(year, site, location, numbsquares, size_mm)
```

#### 4.2 How many limpet territories did we measure?

```{r}
## How many territories were measured at each site in each year? 
Cleaned_Territories_Final |> 
  group_by(site,year) |>
  summarise(n=n())
```

#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

- territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

- Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
# Create a dataset containing calculated territory area and estimated body mass
All_Territories_area_mass <- Cleaned_Territories_Final |> 
  
  # Calculate territory area in square millimeters
  # Each square of the mesh measures 19 mm × 19 mm
  # Multiply the number of squares by the area of one square
  mutate(
    territory_area_mm = numbsquares * (19^2),
    
    # Estimate limpet body mass in grams using shell size
    # Formula: mass (g) = 0.00009 × shell length (mm)^3.0471
    body_mass = 0.00009 * size_mm^3.0471
  )

```

#### 4.4. Is there a relationship between limpet size and territory size?

Explore the relationship between mass_g, and area_mm2 using scatter plots.

```{r}

All_Territories_area_mass |> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes (x=territory_area_mm, y = body_mass) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth (method = lm, se = FALSE) + 
  labs(x = "Territory Area (mm^2)", y = "Mass (g)")
  
```

```{r}

  # Set territory area on the x-axis and body mass on the y-axis
  aes(x = territory_area_mm, y = body_mass) +
  
  # Add points to represent individual observations

    aes(fill = factor(site)), # Fill points according to sampling site
    shape = 21,               # Use circles with separate fill and outline colors
    color = "Pink",           # Set the outline color to pink
    size = 4                  # Set the size of the points
  ) +
  
  # Label the axes and the legend
  labs(
    x = "Territory Area (mm²)", # Territory area in square millimeters
    y = "Mass (g)",             # Estimated body mass in grams
    fill = "Site"               # Legend title for sampling site
  )
 
```

```{r}
# Create a scatter plot of body mass versus territory area,
# with a best-fit regression line and separate panels by habitat
All_Territories_area_mass |>
  ggplot() +
  
  # Set body mass on the x-axis and territory area on the y-axis
  aes(x = body_mass, y = territory_area_mm) +
  
  # Plot individual observations as points
  geom_point() +
  
  # Add a linear regression line using the lm method
  # se = FALSE removes the shaded standard error confidence band
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  
  # Create a separate plot panel for each location or habitat
  facet_wrap(~ location) +
  
  # Label the x-axis and y-axis
  labs(
    x = "Mass (g)",
    y = "Territory Area (mm²)"
  )
```

#### 4.5 What observations do you make about these plots? What do you find interesting about them? Explain one observation and make one more plot of your choosing to explore something you found interesting.

The scatterplots show the relationship between limpet body mass and territory size. I find it interesting that larger limpets may have larger territories, although there is some variation in the data. The plots separated by site can also help show whether this relationship is similar across different locations.

```{r}
 All_Territories_area_mass |>
   ggplot() + 
   aes (x = location, y=territory_area_mm)+ 
   geom_boxplot() + 
   labs (x= "Habitat Location", y = "Territory Area")
```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

```{r}

# write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 

linear_model <- lm(territory_area_mm ~ body_mass, data = All_Territories_area_mass)
plot(linear_model)

```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval

All_Territories_area_mass |> ggplot() + 
  aes(x = log(body_mass), y = log(territory_area_mm)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) + 
  labs( x = "Mass (g)", y = "Territory Area (mm^2)")

```

```{r}
# Fit a linear regression model using log-transformed variables
# Response variable: log of territory area (mm²)
# Explanatory variable: log of body mass (g)
log_model <- lm(
  log(territory_area_mm) ~ log(body_mass),
  data = All_Territories_area_mass
)

# Plot residuals versus fitted values to assess
# linearity and constant variance (homoscedasticity)
plot(log_model, which = 1)

# Create a normal Q-Q plot to assess whether
# the model residuals are approximately normally distributed
plot(log_model, which = 2)
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}
summary(log_model) 

```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**

#### 4.9 Compare the relationship we found to the original study.

```{r}
# Display the Fenberg territory dataset
FenbergTerr

# Plot the Fenberg data using log-transformed variables
FenbergTerr |> 
  ggplot() +
  
  # Set log-transformed mass on the x-axis
  # and log-transformed territory area on the y-axis
  aes(x = log(mass_g), y = log(area_mm2)) +
  
  # Plot individual observations
  geom_point() +
  
  # Add the best-fit linear regression line
  # se = FALSE removes the shaded confidence interval
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  
  # Label the axes
  labs(
    x = "Log Mass (g)",
    y = "Log Territory Area (mm²)"
  )


# Fit a linear regression model to the log-transformed data
Fenberg_model <- lm(log(area_mm2) ~ log(mass_g), data = FenbergTerr)

# Display the model results, including the slope and intercept
summary(Fenberg_model)

# Extract the intercept and slope directly
coef(Fenberg_model)


```
